### v1.9.0 — Foundation embeddings as causal instrumental variables

The **Pillar 1 × Pillar 4 bridge**. Backdoor adjustment (Pillar 1)
identifies causal effects only under **causal sufficiency** — all
confounders observed. When unobserved confounders `U` remain, the
adjusted estimator is biased:

``` math
\hat{\beta}_{\text{backdoor}} = \beta_{\text{true}} + \text{bias}(U)
```

**Instrumental variables** (IVs) identify effects under a different set
of assumptions \[@Wooldridge2010\]:

1.  **Relevance**: $`\text{Cov}(Z, X) \neq 0`$
2.  **Exclusion**: $`Z \to Y`$ only through $`X`$
3.  **Unconfoundedness**: $`Z \perp U`$

The MoCo v2 encoder (Pillar 4), trained contrastively on landscape
patches *without ever seeing SOC*, is a natural IV candidate: it
captures landscape-scale structure orthogonal to the named confounders
in the DAG.

``` r

# 2SLS with foundation-model embeddings as instruments
iv_fit <- edaphos::causal_iv_from_embeddings(
  data       = cerrado_profiles,
  embeddings = foundation_embeddings,    # (n x 128) MoCo v2 output
  exposure   = "map",
  outcome    = "soc",
  covariates = c("mat","slope","elev","clay","sand","bd","trees"),
  n_pcs      = 5L   # top-5 PCs as instruments
)
iv_fit
#> <edaphos_causal_iv>
#>   map -> soc  (estimator: 2SLS, n = 3020)
#>   instruments : PC_1, PC_2, PC_3, PC_4, PC_5
#>   effect      : 0.0039  (OLS 0.0063; backdoor OLS 0.0075)
#>   stage-1 F   : 4630   (instruments very relevant)
#>   Sargan J    : p = 2.0e-17   (over-identification rejected)
```

**Synthetic DGP validation (known truth β = 1.5):**

| Estimator         |        β̂ |       95% CI       |
|:------------------|---------:|:------------------:|
| OLS (biased by U) |     1.82 |   \[1.77, 1.87\]   |
| **2SLS (IV)**     | **1.46** | **\[1.39, 1.53\]** |
| True              |     1.50 |         —          |

The synthetic check confirms the estimator recovers a known truth when
its assumptions hold. The real-data result is a **negative** one, and
that is the point. The MoCo v2 encoder here is real — 7 channels, 12 000
tiles, 3 000 epochs on-device (Metal), InfoNCE 7.2 → 5.2 — not a proxy.
Its embedding PCs are *extremely* relevant instruments (stage-1 F ≈ 1
955, covariate-adjusted 2SLS), yet they decisively **fail the Sargan
over-identification test** (p ≈ 3 × 10⁻¹³). A learned landscape
representation does not manufacture a valid instrument: it encodes
climate, terrain, soil and vegetation together, so it reaches SOC
through many paths and violates the exclusion restriction. This is the
empirical face of [Zhang & Wadoux
(2026)](https://doi.org/10.1111/ejss.70284)’s argument that causal
sufficiency — and, here, instrument validity — is seldom achievable in
DSM from observational data. IV does not rescue identification; the
honest report is the failed test, not a headline effect.

📖 Vignette:
[`vignette("pilar1-pilar4-iv")`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/articles/pilar1-pilar4-iv.md).

### Foundation-model embeddings as instruments: what the Sargan test actually says

Two functions close the loop from the identification argument to
empirical evidence:

- **`foundation_embed_at_coords(moco, coords, stack, dataset, ...)`**
  extracts one embedding per query coordinate by cutting a
  `patch_size x patch_size` window, normalising, and running the encoder
  forward — 17 s for 1 095 WoSIS profiles on Apple M1 Max MPS.
- **`foundation_build_cerrado_stack(bbox, ...)`** assembles the
  31-channel SoilGrids + WorldClim + SRTM stack the encoder was trained
  on (measured: 1.84 GB downloaded, 3.0 min, cached to disk).

Using the Zenodo-published `edaphos-cerrado-moco-v1` encoder on the 1
095 Cerrado profiles, at the encoder’s native 0.01-deg grid:

| Exposure         | Stage-1 F |  Sargan p | Over-identification |
|:-----------------|----------:|----------:|:--------------------|
| MAP → SOC        |   **862** | **0.250** | not rejected        |
| Tree cover → SOC |       8.4 |     0.042 | rejected            |
| Clay → SOC       |      11.0 |    0.0030 | rejected            |

**The result is partial, and that is the finding.** For mean annual
precipitation the instruments are strong (F = 862) and the
over-identification restriction is not rejected: an encoder pretrained
by contrastive self-supervision *without ever seeing SOC* does yield
structurally valid instruments for that exposure, and the 2SLS estimate
(β = 0.0126) is 64 % larger than the backdoor-OLS estimate (β = 0.0077),
the direction expected when attenuation from covariate measurement error
is corrected.

For tree cover and clay the same instruments fail. Tree cover also has a
first-stage F of 8.4, below the conventional threshold of 10, so its
2SLS estimate should not be read as identified at all. Clay’s Sargan p =
0.003 rejects exclusion outright.

**Three limitations that bound every number above.**

1.  *The encoder’s training normalisation was never persisted.* The
    weights registry has no per-channel mean/sd for
    `edaphos-cerrado-moco-v1`, so the exact standardisation it was
    trained under is unrecoverable. The figures above use per-channel
    statistics computed over this area of interest, which is an
    approximation, not a reconstruction. The bundle records this as
    `normalisation_source = "aoi"`. Every future encoder must publish
    its statistics; the registry now carries a `norm_stats_status` field
    so the gap is visible rather than assumed away.
2.  *The area of interest exceeds the training region.* The WoSIS
    profiles span 18.4° × 21.9°; the encoder was trained on the Cerrado
    core, 10° × 13°. The bundle records `aoi_exceeds_training = TRUE`.
    21.8 % of the encoder’s 64 backbone channels are dead (exactly zero
    after post-ReLU average pooling) on this input, against roughly 5 %
    for input drawn from the distribution it was trained on.
3.  *These are single-run values.* Sargan p = 0.042 for tree cover sits
    close enough to 0.05 that it should not be treated as a sharp
    verdict without a resampling study.

Earlier releases of this README reported Sargan p of 0.343 / 0.283 /
0.424 for the three exposures and concluded that the test passed for all
of them. Those figures were produced with the normalisation placeholder
`means = 0`, `sds = 1`, which fed raw geophysical magnitudes into a
network trained on standardised inputs and killed about half its
channels. They have been withdrawn and replaced by the table above.
`tests/testthat/test-headline-claims.R` now asserts every figure in this
section against the shipped `inst/extdata/causal_iv_cerrado_real.rds`,
so the two cannot drift apart again.

### v1.9.2 — Cinelli & Hazlett (2020) sensitivity analysis

The Sargan test validates instrument *exclusion*; sensitivity analysis
quantifies *robustness to residual confounding* after the fact.
Following \[@CinelliHazlett2020\] we compute the **Robustness Value
(RV)**: the minimum partial R² that an unobserved confounder would need
to have with *both* X and Y to zero out the estimate.

``` r

# Any of the following produces a RV summary
s <- edaphos::causal_sensitivity_summary(effect = 0.00769,
                                           se     = 0.00271,
                                           df     = 1084)
s$rv         # -> 0.083   (8.3% of residual variance)
s$rv_alpha   # -> 0.026   (threshold for significance loss)

# Or wrap an `lm` / `edaphos_causal_iv`:
edaphos::causal_sensitivity_from_lm(fit, exposure = "map")
edaphos::causal_sensitivity_from_iv(iv_fit)
```

**Robustness table on the 1 095 Cerrado profiles:**

| Exposure     | Estimator             |      β̂ |    **RV** | RV @ 5% |
|:-------------|:----------------------|-------:|----------:|--------:|
| MAP (mm/a)   | Naive OLS             | 0.0072 |  **9.2%** |    3.7% |
| MAP (mm/a)   | Backdoor OLS          | 0.0077 |  **8.3%** |    2.6% |
| MAP (mm/a)   | Proxy IV (v1.9.0)     | 0.0081 |  **8.6%** |    3.0% |
| MAP (mm/a)   | Real MoCo IV (v1.9.1) | 0.0169 |  **3.9%** |    0.0% |
| Tree cover   | Backdoor OLS          |   6.54 |  **6.3%** |    0.5% |
| Tree cover   | Real MoCo IV          |   4.98 |  **0.9%** |    0.0% |
| **Clay (%)** | Naive OLS             |  0.526 | **24.4%** |   19.8% |
| Clay (%)     | Backdoor OLS          |  0.192 |  **5.0%** |    0.0% |
| Clay (%)     | Real MoCo IV          |  0.858 |  **3.9%** |    0.0% |

**Scientific finding.** *The only robust causal claim in the Cerrado
stack is Clay → SOC under Naive OLS* (RV = 24%): no plausible confounder
explaining less than a quarter of the residual variance could zero it
out. MAP → SOC under Backdoor OLS is moderately robust (RV ≈ 8%); under
real-encoder IV it drops to ≈ 4%, because the synthetic-stack mode
yields weak instruments (Stage-1 F ≈ 10) and an inflated SE. A
real-covariate run should lift F and reduce the SE, restoring RV — but
note that the `EDAPHOS_IV_REAL_STACK` switch this README once told
readers to set is read nowhere in the package. The real-stack path is a
roadmap item, not a flag.

The package was validated against the published Cinelli-Hazlett Theorem
4.4 example to four decimal places (RV = 0.1810 expected, 0.1810
computed).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Pillar 2 — Physics-Informed ML

### Motivation

Classical depth-harmonisation uses **equal-area splines** \[[Bishop et
al. 1999](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0016-7061(99)00003-8)\] — a purely
mathematical object disconnected from pedogenesis. Pillar 2 replaces the
spline with a *physics-informed* kinetic of clay illuviation /
organic-matter decay, parameterised either analytically or by a neural
network and integrated end-to-end.

**Alignment with [Zhang & Wadoux
(2026)](https://doi.org/10.1111/ejss.70284).** The pedogenetic ODE is
the closest this package comes to their **generative causality**: the
soil property arises from a process the modeller writes down, which is
their condition 1 (an explicit model). It does *not* satisfy their
condition 3, faithfulness — that is a property of the data relative to a
graph, not of an equation, and the DAG this package ships fails its own
implied-independence test (see
[`causal_dag_test()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/causal_dag_test.md)).
Earlier versions of this README claimed both conditions; the claim about
faithfulness was a category error.

Note also that the equation in this section is not itself derived from a
process: it is the Russell & Moore (1968) exponential depth function
with a fourth shape parameter.
[`piml_profile_fit_mechanistic()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/piml_profile_fit_mechanistic.md)
is the derived alternative, from the steady-state advection-reaction
balance, and on real multi-horizon profiles it is also the more accurate
of the two.

### Governing object

Depth-dependent translocation toward an equilibrium coordinate
$`y_\infty`$ — which, because the rate decays with depth, is **not** the
value the profile reaches (see the note below the equation),

``` math
\frac{dy}{dz} \;=\; -\,\lambda_0\,e^{-\mu z}\,\bigl(y(z) - y_\infty\bigr)
\qquad\text{(parametric)}
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\frac{dy}{dz} \;=\; f_\theta\bigl(z, y, \mathbf{x}\bigr)
\qquad\text{(Neural ODE).}
```

The **parametric** form is separable, so it is solved in closed form
rather than integrated numerically, and fitted through a horizon-average
observation operator; the **Neural ODE** form uses a fixed-step
Runge-Kutta integrator in `torch` so training back-propagates through
the whole trajectory \[[Chen et
al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.07366)\].

### Point and Bayesian APIs

``` r

data(sp4, package = "aqp")
sp4$depth <- (sp4$top + sp4$bottom) / 2
colusa <- subset(sp4, id == "colusa")

# Point estimate
param  <- piml_profile_fit(colusa$depth, colusa$clay)

# Bayesian posterior. Laplace is the fast default; MCMC is what the paper
# reports, because on a real pedon Laplace narrows 5 of 7 intervals -- the
# observation noise by 1.8x -- being Gaussian on the log coordinates.
fit    <- piml_profile_fit_bayesian(colusa$depth, colusa$clay,
                                     method = "mcmc", seed = 1L)

# Neural ODE
neural <- piml_neural_ode_fit(
  colusa$depth, colusa$clay,
  hidden = c(16L, 16L), epochs = 500L, seed = 1L
)

# Deep ensemble (K = 5) — canonical uncertainty for the Neural ODE
ens <- piml_neural_ode_fit_ensemble(colusa$depth, colusa$clay, K = 5L)

predict(fit, newdepths = c(10, 20, 40, 80),
        interval = 0.95, include_obs_noise = TRUE, seed = 1L)
```

The fitted parameters carry pedological meaning — `y0 ≈ 19 %` is the
clay extrapolated to the surface, `mu` says whether translocation
accelerates or slows with depth — but this pedon also shows the limit of
that reading. Its four horizons stop at 42 cm and the clay is *still
rising*, so the model has no information about where the argillic
horizon levels off, and [`print()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/print.html)
says so:

      NOTE: the deepest horizon (36 cm) has travelled only 0% of the
            way to y(Inf), so the deep value is an extrapolation, not an
            estimate. Do not read it as a parent-material value.

Earlier versions of this README quoted `y_inf ≈ 62 %` here and called it
the argillic asymptote. That number was not estimated from the data: the
L2 penalty was applied to the raw `y_inf`, so it scaled with the square
of the property’s units and pinned the value. Removing the penalty on
the same four horizons gives 533 %. The regulariser is now a scale-free
shrinkage toward the observed range, and an unidentified asymptote is
reported as unidentified. To estimate a parent-material value you need
horizons deep enough to see the profile flatten.

The Neural ODE fits the same four horizons to tighter RMSE and is the
default for non-monotonic profiles (E-below-A, buried paleosols).

![Clay depth profile for the colusa pedon — parametric ODE and Neural
ODE fits with uncertainty bands](reference/figures/pillar2-piml.png)

### Closing the Pillar 2 × Pillar 5 loop

[`al_physics_gate_piml()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/al_physics_gate_piml.md)
takes any PIML fit and turns it into a **rejection gate** that the
Pillar 5 Active Learning loop uses to discard candidates whose predicted
profile violates monotonicity, non-negativity, or plausible-range
constraints. This is the concrete implementation of the
“process-informed filter” that [Zhang & Wadoux
(2026)](https://doi.org/10.1111/ejss.70284) advocate: model candidates
aren’t just ranked by statistical uncertainty but also by *physical
plausibility*.

📖 Vignette:
[`vignette("pilar2-piml-profile")`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/articles/pilar2-piml-profile.md).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Pillar 3 — 4D Pedometry

### Motivation

Most digital soil maps report a time-invariant field, which is
ecologically false: topsoil SOC responds measurably to climate forcing
on monthly-to-annual scales \[[Lehmann and Kleber
2015](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature16069); [Minasny et
al. 2017](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.geoderma.2017.01.002)\]. [Zhang and
Wadoux (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1111/ejss.70284) explicitly flag this
as a weakness of successionist DSM: *“soil measurements and observations
capture only a snapshot emerging from a complex, dynamic system, without
clear temporal sequencing.”*

Pillar 3 adds the time dimension with a **stacked Convolutional LSTM**
\[[Shi et al. 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.04214)\] and a
**stochastic Ensemble Kalman Filter** \[[Evensen
1994](https://doi.org/10.1029/94JC00572)\] for assimilating new in-situ
observations.

### Governing object

A multi-layer ConvLSTM propagates a spatial hidden state
$`\mathbf{H}_t`$ and cell state $`\mathbf{C}_t`$ alongside time:

``` math
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{i}_t &= \sigma\bigl(W_{xi} * \mathbf{X}_t + W_{hi} * \mathbf{H}_{t-1}\bigr), \\
\mathbf{f}_t &= \sigma\bigl(W_{xf} * \mathbf{X}_t + W_{hf} * \mathbf{H}_{t-1}\bigr), \\
\mathbf{g}_t &= \tanh\bigl(W_{xg} * \mathbf{X}_t + W_{hg} * \mathbf{H}_{t-1}\bigr), \\
\mathbf{o}_t &= \sigma\bigl(W_{xo} * \mathbf{X}_t + W_{ho} * \mathbf{H}_{t-1}\bigr), \\
\mathbf{C}_t &= \mathbf{f}_t \odot \mathbf{C}_{t-1} + \mathbf{i}_t \odot \mathbf{g}_t, \\
\mathbf{H}_t &= \mathbf{o}_t \odot \tanh(\mathbf{C}_t),
\end{aligned}
```

with `*` a 2-D convolution and `⊙` the Hadamard product.

### Example

``` r

cube   <- temporal_synth_soc_cube(H = 12L, W = 12L, T_total = 18L, seed = 7L)
past   <- temporal_cube_to_tensor(cube, t_slice = 1:12)
future <- temporal_cube_to_tensor(cube, t_slice = 13:18)

fit <- temporal_convlstm_fit(
  past$sequence, past$target,
  hidden_dims     = c(12L, 6L),        # stacked ConvLSTM
  kernel_size     = 3L,
  return_sequence = TRUE,
  epochs          = 120L, lr = 0.02,
  seed            = 1L
)
forecast <- temporal_convlstm_rollout(
  fit,
  past_sequence  = past$sequence,
  future_drivers = future$sequence
)
```

![Observed vs. ConvLSTM-forecast monthly SOC trajectory at a
pixel](reference/figures/pillar3-4d.png)

### 🎯 Stochastic EnKF with Gaspari-Cohn localization (v1.5.0)

In a realistic DSM pipeline, new in-situ observations keep arriving
**after** the ConvLSTM was trained.
[`temporal_kalman_update()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/temporal_kalman_update.md)
nudges the trained forecast toward those new observations with a
stochastic Ensemble Kalman Filter \[[Evensen
1994](https://doi.org/10.1029/94JC00572); [Burgers, van Leeuwen and
Evensen
1998](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0493(1998)126%3C1719:ASITEK%3E2.0.CO;2)\]:
a gain matrix is estimated directly from the ensemble sample covariance
and applied per-member, so the posterior ensemble reflects the new
evidence without retraining.

The default localization is **Gaspari-Cohn** — a compactly supported
5th-order polynomial that tapers the gain smoothly to zero at twice the
specified radius, preventing spurious long-range correlations typical of
small ensembles.

``` r

fc_ens <- array(..., dim = c(K = 10, H = 10, W = 10))

assim <- temporal_kalman_update(
  forecast_ensemble   = fc_ens,
  obs_value           = c(0.62, 0.58, 0.51),
  obs_row             = c(5L, 10L, 15L),
  obs_col             = c(5L, 10L, 15L),
  obs_sd              = 0.02,
  localization_radius = 2                    # Gaspari-Cohn taper
)
```

### Real-data demonstration (v1.5.0)

The bundled `temporal_cerrado_results.rds` holds the full pipeline run
on a **real Cerrado 2° × 2° AoI cube** (MOD13Q1 NDVI + NASA POWER
precipitation + NASA POWER T2M, 168 monthly steps, 2003 – 2016), with:

- 10 × 10 grid at 0.2° resolution
- K = 10-member ConvLSTM ensemble
- 8 synthetic in-situ observations for the EnKF test
- localization radius = 2 cells

| Metric | Prior (ConvLSTM) | Analysis (EnKF + localization) | Reduction |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| RMSE (COS, normalised) | 0.637 | **0.617** | **−3.2%** |

The Kalman gain map becomes the first priority signal for the Pillar 5
active-learning loop — cells with large gain would benefit most from
*another* in-situ sample.

📖 Vignette:
[`vignette("pilar3-4d-soc")`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/articles/pilar3-4d-soc.md).
The real-AoI run above is distributed as a result bundle rather than as
a vignette.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Pillar 4 — Foundation Models

### Motivation

Labelled soil samples are expensive; covariate rasters are abundant.
Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) \[[Chen et
al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.05709); [Jean et
al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.02855)\] pre-trains an encoder on
*unlabelled* raster patches and reuses the resulting representation as a
learned feature map — the premise of a future “**SoilGPT**”.

### Governing object

For each batch of $`B`$ raster patches, SimCLR draws two stochastic
augmentations per patch, encodes each with a shared backbone CNN and
projection head, and minimises the **normalised temperature-scaled
cross-entropy** loss \[[Chen et
al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.05709)\]:

``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\text{NT-Xent}}
\;=\;
-\frac{1}{2B}
\sum_{i=1}^{B}\sum_{v\in\{1,2\}}
\log
\frac{\exp\!\bigl(\mathrm{sim}(\mathbf{z}^{(v)}_{i},\,\mathbf{z}^{(v')}_{i}) / \tau\bigr)}
     {\displaystyle\sum_{k \neq (i,v)} \exp\!\bigl(\mathrm{sim}(\mathbf{z}^{(v)}_{i},\,\mathbf{z}_{k})/\tau\bigr)}.
```

After pre-training the **projection head is discarded** and the backbone
output $`f_\theta(\mathbf{x})`$ is reused as the downstream feature
vector. MoCo v2 \[[He et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.05722);
[Chen et al. 2020b](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.04297)\] replaces the
two-view symmetric loss with a queue-based momentum encoder, scaling to
larger batches.

### Zenodo-hosted pre-trained weights

``` r

moco <- foundation_weights_load("edaphos-cerrado-moco-v1", verbose = TRUE)
fit  <- foundation_fit_classifier(
  moco, labelled_patches, soil_order,
  freeze_backbone = TRUE, head = "linear",
  epochs = 40L, device = "mps", seed = 1L
)
predict(fit, new_patches, type = "prob")
```

The first published encoder — **`edaphos-cerrado-moco-v1`** — was
pre-trained on Apple M1 Max (MPS) over 50 000 16 × 16 tiles of a core
Cerrado AoI (longitude −53 to −43, latitude −23 to −10), stacking
SoilGrids 250 m, WorldClim 2.1 and SRTM 30-arc-second. Zenodo DOI
[10.5281/zenodo.19701276](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19701276). An
encoder `v2` (200 k steps, 10× the v1 budget) is currently in training;
v1.3.2 will re-benchmark with the new weights.

### 🔀 Deep-ensemble + MC-dropout (v1.6.0)

Pillar 4 was deterministic through v1.5.0. v1.6.0 ships two canonical
uncertainty recipes:

- **`foundation_finetune_ensemble(K = 5L)`** — K independent heads on
  the same encoder, different seeds \[[Lakshminarayanan et
  al. 2017](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/7219-simple-and-scalable-predictive-uncertainty-estimation-using-deep-ensembles)\].
- **[`foundation_mcdropout_predict()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/foundation_mcdropout_predict.md)**
  — N Monte-Carlo dropout forward passes with the dropout layers left
  active at predict time \[[Gal and Ghahramani
  2016](http://proceedings.mlr.press/v48/gal16.md)\].

Both wrap into an `edaphos_posterior`, so
[`uncertainty_calibrate()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/uncertainty_calibrate.md)
applies identically.

📖 Vignette:
[`vignette("pilar4-simclr-embeddings")`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/articles/pilar4-simclr-embeddings.md).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Pillar 5 — Autonomous Active Learning

### Motivation

Traditional DSM decouples sampling design from model fitting — a
pre-defined scheme collects observations, then a model is trained on
whatever landed. This discards the fact that, once an initial model
exists, its **uncertainty field** is direct guidance on where additional
information is most needed \[[Settles
2009](http://digital.library.wisc.edu/1793/60660); [Brus
2019](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.geoderma.2018.07.036)\]. Pillar 5 closes
the loop: **fit → query → measure → refit**.

### Governing object

A hybrid batch-mode acquisition policy,

``` math
\pi_{\text{hyb}}(\mathbf{x};\alpha)
 \;=\;\alpha\,\tilde{u}_t(\mathbf{x}) \;+\; (1-\alpha)\,\tilde{d}_t(\mathbf{x}),
\qquad \alpha\in[0,1],
```

where $`\tilde{u}_t`$ is the **Quantile Regression Forest**
\[[Meinshausen
2006](https://jmlr.csail.mit.edu/papers/v7/meinshausen06a.html)\]
prediction-interval width and $`\tilde{d}_t`$ is the min-distance
feature-space diversity from the already-labelled set. A `"cost"`
variant adds a logistical-distance penalty for autonomous sampler
deployment; a `physics_gate` keyword rejects physically implausible
candidates via a PIML fit (the Pillar 2 × 5 bridge).

### Example

``` r

covs <- c("elev", "slope", "twi", "map_mm", "ndvi")

set.seed(42)
seed_idx <- al_initial_design(br_cerrado, covariates = covs, n = 25L, iter = 1500L)

set.seed(42)
model <- al_loop(
  labeled    = br_cerrado[ seed_idx, ],
  candidates = br_cerrado[-seed_idx, ],
  target     = "soc", covariates = covs,
  coords     = c("x", "y"),
  budget     = 45L, batch = 5L,
  strategy   = "hybrid", alpha = 0.7,
  num.trees  = 500L, verbose = FALSE
)
tail(al_history(model), 5)
#>    iter n_labeled rmse_oob mean_uncertainty
#> 6     5        50 5.387328          20.1760
#> 7     6        55 5.376662          19.1320
#> 8     7        60 5.294309          19.1900
#> 9     8        65 4.913287          18.3640
#> 10    9        70 4.942248          16.9916
```

![OOB RMSE decreasing as the AL loop adds
samples](reference/figures/pillar5-al-learning.png)![Spatial
distribution of cLHS seed and AL-queried
points](reference/figures/pillar5-al-map.png)

OOB RMSE falls from 5.37 to 4.94 g/kg after nine batches of 5 samples.
Queried points concentrate in transition zones between covariate regimes
— exactly where expert pedologists historically placed transects.

### 🎲 BatchBALD (v1.1.0)

An information-theoretic alternative to the hybrid heuristic:
[`al_query_batchbald()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/al_query_batchbald.md)
picks the batch that maximises the mutual information between its labels
and the model parameters \[[Kirsch et
al. 2019](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/9357-batchbald-efficient-and-diverse-batch-acquisition-for-deep-bayesian-active-learning)\]:

``` math
\mathrm{BatchBALD}(B) \;=\; I(y_B; \theta \mid x_B, \mathcal D).
```

For a QRF (the
[`al_fit()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/al_fit.md)
backbone) the trees are the parameter samples, so the joint covariance
of the epistemic posterior is the per-tree empirical covariance across
candidates. Under Gaussian aleatoric noise $`\sigma_a^2`$ the objective
reduces to a log-determinant with a $`(1 - 1/e)`$ optimality guarantee
\[[Nemhauser et al. 1978](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01588971)\].
Incremental Cholesky / Schur-complement updates make every greedy step
$`O(m^2 \cdot n_{\text{pool}})`$.

📖 Vignette:
[`vignette("pilar5-active-learning")`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/articles/pilar5-active-learning.md).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Pillar 6 — Quantum ML

### Motivation

High-dimensional covariate stacks eventually hit the classical **curse
of dimensionality**. Pillar 6 reformulates the kernel of the regression
problem as the **overlap of parametrised quantum states** \[[Havlicek et
al. 2019](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-0980-2); [Schuld and
Killoran 2019](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.122.040504)\], living
in a Hilbert space of dimension $`2^n`$ in the number of qubits yet
classically simulable in pure R for $`n \le 8`$.

> **What it does on this repository’s own benchmark.** Fifth of six
> methods, RMSE 0.663 against 0.586 for ordinary least squares on
> DAG-selected covariates, and an NSE of −0.019 — that is, marginally
> *worse* than predicting the training-fold mean everywhere. The
> construction below is sound and the implementation is verified against
> a reference, but on this data set the quantum kernel does not buy
> accuracy, and the pillar is presented as a method that is available
> rather than one that is recommended. The four-way head-to-head later
> in this section reaches the same conclusion from a different angle.

### Governing object

The ZZFeatureMap quantum state

``` math
\lvert\phi(\mathbf{x})\rangle \;=\;
  \bigl(U_\phi(\mathbf{x})\,H^{\otimes n}\bigr)^{R}\,\lvert 0\rangle^{\otimes n}
```

induces the kernel

``` math
K(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j) \;=\;
  \bigl\lvert \langle \phi(\mathbf{x}_j) \mid \phi(\mathbf{x}_i)\rangle \bigr\rvert^{2},
```

with

``` math
U_\phi(\mathbf{x}) \;=\; \exp\!\Bigl(i\!\sum_{S\subseteq[n]} \phi_S(\mathbf{x})\!\prod_{i\in S}\! Z_i\Bigr),
\quad
\phi_{\{i\}}(\mathbf{x}) = 2\,x_i,
\quad
\phi_{\{i,j\}}(\mathbf{x}) = 2\,(\pi - x_i)(\pi - x_j).
```

### GP-equivalent posterior (v1.6.0)

Using the well-known equivalence between Kernel Ridge Regression and
Gaussian-process regression \[Rasmussen & Williams 2006 §2.3\], the
Q-KRR’s predictive variance is analytic:

``` math
\sigma_\epsilon^2(\mathbf{x}_\star) = \underbrace{k(\mathbf{x}_\star, \mathbf{x}_\star)}_{\text{aleatoric}} - \underbrace{k(\mathbf{x}_\star, X)\,(K + \lambda I)^{-1}\,k(X, \mathbf{x}_\star)}_{\text{epistemic}} + \sigma_n^2
```

where $`\sigma_n^2`$ is the leave-one-out residual variance.
[`quantum_krr_posterior()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/quantum_krr_posterior.md)
wraps this into an `edaphos_posterior` with the epistemic / aleatoric
decomposition carried through the object.

### Qiskit VQE pipeline (v0.9.0)

Three interchangeable execution backends for variational quantum
eigensolvers:

``` r

ham <- quantum_hamiltonian_h2()

# 1) Exact noiseless statevector
quantum_vqe_fit(ham, backend = "aer_statevector", seed = 1L)

# 2) Shot-based Aer simulation with SPSA
quantum_vqe_fit(ham, backend = "aer_shots",
                shots = 4096L, optimizer = "SPSA",
                max_iter = 80L, seed = 1L)

# 3) Real IBM Quantum hardware with M3 readout mitigation
Sys.setenv(IBMQ_TOKEN = "<your-ibm-quantum-api-token>")
quantum_vqe_fit(ham, backend = "ibmq",
                ibmq_backend = "ibm_brisbane",
                shots = 8192L, mitigation = "m3",
                optimizer = "SPSA", max_iter = 50L)
```

Three organo-mineral Hamiltonians come pre-built via qiskit-nature +
PySCF:

| Variant | Pedological role | Active space | Qubits |
|:---|:---|:--:|:--:|
| `"formic_acid"` | carboxylate — dominant humic functional group | (2e, 2o) | 2 |
| `"methanediol"` | ortho-diol — catechol-style Fe(III) chelator | (2e, 2o) | 2 |
| `"ferric_formate"` | monodentate Fe(III)–OOCH — minimum viable organo-mineral | (4e, 4o) | 4 |

![Heatmap of the quantum kernel Gram matrix on 70 Cerrado
samples](reference/figures/pillar6-quantum.png)

📖 Vignette:
[`vignette("pilar6-quantum")`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/articles/pilar6-quantum.md).

### v2.0.0 — Quantum kernel over foundation-model embeddings

The **Pilar 4 × Pilar 6 fusion**. Foundation embeddings (64-dim MoCo v2
outputs) are compressed to `n_pcs` principal components rescaled to
$`[-\pi, \pi]`$, then lifted into a $`2^n`$-dimensional Hilbert space by
the ZZFeatureMap. Four new exported functions:

``` r

# 1. Reduce foundation embeddings to top-n PCs in quantum range
red <- edaphos::qf_embed_reduce(embeddings, n_pcs = 6L)

# 2. Compare quantum, RBF, and linear Gram matrices
cmp <- edaphos::qf_kernel_compare(red$X_q, reps = 2L)
cmp$diagnostics   # Frobenius distance + effective rank

# 3. Fit Quantum-KRR directly on foundation embeddings
fit <- edaphos::qf_krr_fit(embeddings, y,
                            n_pcs = 6L, reps = 2L, lambda = 0.5)

# 4. 4-way head-to-head benchmark
bm <- edaphos::qf_krr_benchmark(embeddings, covariates, y,
                                  n_pcs = 6L, reps = 2L, lambda = 0.5)
```

**This benchmark is a negative control.** The raster stack the encoder
sees is white noise —
[`stats::rnorm()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/Normal.html) into every cell
of every channel (`data-raw/quantum_foundation_benchmark.R`) — so the
“foundation embeddings” describe a landscape that carries no signal, by
construction. Three of the four methods below predict from features that
*cannot* contain information about SOC. Read it as a check that the
pipeline reports failure when there is nothing to find, not as a
covariate benchmark. For the real-covariate answer see the six-method
table below.

**5-fold spatial CV on 1 081 Cerrado profiles (synthetic-stack mode).**
The Cerrado pool holds 1 095 profiles; 14 lose their embedding at the
[`complete.cases()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/complete.cases.html) step
after the encoder pass, so the CV runs on 1 081. This table said 1 095
until the bundle was re-read.

| Method                        | RMSE | MAE | R² (pooled) | R² (fold mean) |
|:------------------------------|-----:|----:|------------:|---------------:|
| Quantum KRR on raw covariates | 15.5 | 9.2 |      −0.075 |         −0.350 |
| ranger (raw covariates)       | 15.5 | 9.0 |      −0.075 |         −0.795 |
| Quantum KRR on foundation PCs | 15.6 | 9.3 |      −0.089 |         −0.295 |
| RBF-KRR on foundation PCs     | 16.1 | 9.8 |      −0.159 |         −0.449 |

**Finding: all four are worse than predicting the mean.** Every pooled
R² is negative, so no method here beats the zero-parameter null — and
that includes the classical `ranger` baseline, which is the honest
result on noise features. The four are close to one another (−0.075 to
−0.159) and the differences between them are not worth interpreting.

**What this table used to say, and why.** Until this run it read `0.00`
for the three kernel methods and `0.08` for `ranger`, under the
conclusion that the four regressors were *statistically
indistinguishable* and that the quantum lift *matched but did not
surpass* ranger. Those zeros were not measured.
[`qf_krr_benchmark()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/qf_krr_benchmark.md)
computed `max(0, 1 - SS_res/SS_tot)`, so every negative R² — 17 of the
20 fold-by-method values — was floored to exactly zero, which converts
“worse than the mean” into “explains none of the variance”. Two
different findings, and the clamp published the flattering one. The
clamp is gone (`R/quantum_foundation.R` delegates to
[`edaphos_r2()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/edaphos_r2.md),
which is Nash–Sutcliffe and unclamped) and the bundle has been rebuilt
from the same script and seed.

**Two R² columns, because one of them is unstable.**
[`edaphos_r2()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/edaphos_r2.md)
is Nash–Sutcliffe against each test fold’s *own* mean, so a fold whose
profiles happen to be homogeneous has a small denominator and a wild R².
Fold 2 of this partition has sd(SOC) = 5.9 g/kg against 11–21 in the
other four; `ranger` scores −4.28 there, and that single fold drags its
fold-mean to −0.80 and makes it look like the worst of the four. Pooled
over folds — one ratio of summed squares rather than a mean of ratios —
`ranger` is −0.075, mid-pack. The pooled column is the one to read; the
fold mean is shown so the instability is visible instead of smoothed
away.

Earlier versions of this section listed three “testable explanations”
for the null result — a synthetic stack, an undertrained encoder, too
few qubits — and left them standing as though they were reasons to
expect a different answer later. They are not. Each is a reason the run
was *uninformative*; none is evidence that a corrected run would favour
the quantum kernel. Two of the three have since been run, and both
answered against it.

| Proposed test | Status | Result |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **1.** Real covariate stack instead of synthetic | **Run** | Negative. The six-method benchmark (`inst/extdata/benchmark_wosis_6pilar.rds`) scores quantum KRR on the real SoilGrids / WorldClim / SRTM covariates over 1,095 WoSIS profiles and 5 spatially blocked folds with a 68 km buffer: RMSE 0.663 against 0.583 for DAG-restricted OLS, **NSE −0.024** — below the achievable null of the training-fold mean — and PICP90 0.663 against a nominal 0.90. It is also the most expensive method by a factor of 337 (762 s against 2.3 s). |
| **2.** Encoder trained 10× longer (`moco-v2`, 200k steps) | **Run** | Negative, indirectly. Foundation embeddings do reach the benchmark, as P4, and rank **fourth of six** (RMSE 0.616, NSE 0.118) — below both plain OLS and a quantile forest on raw covariates. The embedding route does not carry information the covariates lack; see the instrumental-variable result, where those embeddings are extremely *relevant* and decisively *invalid*. |
| **3.** 8–10 qubits instead of 6 | **Not run** | Open. We do not claim it would fail; we claim nothing about it, which is the honest position for an experiment nobody has done. |

**The contribution is infrastructure.** `qf_*` functions formalise the
Pilar 4 × Pilar 6 fusion and ship a reproducible benchmark. That
benchmark has now been run on real inputs and returned a negative
result, which is reported here rather than deferred to a future version.

📖 Vignette:
[`vignette("pilar4-pilar6-quantum")`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/articles/pilar4-pilar6-quantum.md).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Pillar 7 — Bayesian Hierarchical Spatial

### Motivation

A machine-learning soil map returns a number per pixel; it rarely
returns an honest interval, because residual spatial structure is
treated as noise rather than as a signal with a covariance. Pillar 7
puts the dependence *inside* the model as a Gaussian-process random
effect and returns a posterior over every quantity of interest
\[[Banerjee et al. 2014](https://doi.org/10.1201/b17115)\].

### Governing object

``` math
y = X\beta + w + \varepsilon, \qquad
w \sim GP\big(0,\ \sigma^2 R(\phi)\big), \qquad
\varepsilon \sim N(0,\ \tau^2 I),
```

with $`R(\phi)_{ij} = \exp(-\phi \lVert s_i - s_j \rVert)`$. Note that
$`\phi`$ is a **rate** (units 1/distance), not a range; the practical
correlation range is $`\approx 3/\phi`$.

Conditional on $`\phi`$ every update is conjugate, so
[`bhs_fit()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/bhs_fit.md)
profiles $`\phi`$ by maximum likelihood over `phi_range` and runs a
Metropolis-free Gibbs sampler for everything else — the same concession
INLA makes \[[Rue et
al. 2009](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9868.2008.00700.x)\]. The
Cholesky-heavy inner loop runs through an RcppArmadillo backend.

``` r

fit <- bhs_fit(train, soc ~ elev + slope + twi, coords = c("x", "y"),
               nmcmc = 1500L, burn = 500L, phi_range = c(0.05, 1000))

pred <- predict(fit, newdata = test)   # Bayesian kriging, per draw
```

[`bhs_fit()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/bhs_fit.md)
**warns when the profile-MLE of $`\phi`$ lands on an endpoint of
`phi_range`**: the bracket rather than the data then set the correlation
rate, and the spatial variance fraction is not interpretable. Read that
warning before reading anything else — the vignette shows a case where
the fraction reads 0.97 with a tight posterior in a fit that has no
resolvable spatial field at all.

📖 Vignette:
[`vignette("pilar7-bayesian-hierarchical")`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/articles/pilar7-bayesian-hierarchical.md).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Pillar 8 — Neural Operators

### Motivation

A soil profile is not a stack of independent points; it is a *function*
of depth. Pillar 8 learns the operator that produced it, rather than a
pointwise regression evaluated at fixed depths.

### Governing object

``` math
\mathcal{G} : u(z) \longmapsto y(z)
```

Two architectures, both shipped:

**Fourier Neural Operator** \[[Li et
al. 2021](https://openreview.net/forum?id=c8P9NQVtmnO)\] — spectral
convolution with the spectrum truncated to `n_modes`:

``` math
(\mathcal{K}v)(z) = \mathcal{F}^{-1}\big(R_\theta \cdot \mathcal{F}v\big)(z)
```

**DeepONet** \[[Lu et
al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-021-00302-5)\] — branch/trunk
factorisation, the constructive form of the Chen and Chen (1995)
universal operator approximation theorem:

``` math
\mathcal{G}(u)(z) \approx \sum_{k=1}^{p} b_k(u)\, t_k(z)
```

``` r

don <- no_deeponet_fit(depths, targets, covariates,
                       branch_hidden = 24L, trunk_hidden = 24L)

# The trunk accepts any depth, including ones never trained on:
predict(don, new_covariates, newdepths = c(7.5, 33, 61, 97, 133))
```

That last line is the point of the pillar. On the training grid a
quantile regression forest is at least as accurate; asked for depths it
never saw, it is not. The vignette measures both.

📖 Vignette:
[`vignette("pilar8-neural-operators")`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/articles/pilar8-neural-operators.md).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Pillar 9 — Diffusion Models

### Motivation

Every other pillar answers “what is the value here?”. None answers “what
does a plausible soil landscape look like?” — a map assembled from
per-pixel quantiles is smoother than any real landscape and corresponds
to no coherent realisation. Pillar 9 samples whole maps.

### Governing object

Forward process (fixed, no parameters), on the cosine schedule of
\[[Nichol and Dhariwal
2021](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v139/nichol21a.html)\]:

``` math
q(x_t \mid x_0) = N\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0,\ (1 - \bar\alpha_t) I\big)
```

Only the denoiser $`\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)`$ is learned, by score
matching \[[Ho et
al. 2020](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2020/hash/4c5bcfec8584af0d967f1ab10179ca4b-Abstract.html)\];
[`dm_sample()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/dm_sample.md)
then runs ancestral sampling from $`t = T`$ down to $`0`$ with $`x_0`$
clipping.

``` r

sch <- dm_cosine_schedule(T = 100L)
fit <- dm_fit(patch_stack, T = 100L, epochs = 250L)
gen <- dm_sample(fit, n_samples = 4L)
```

**Honest status.** The pure-R backend trains a readout over frozen
random features (an ELM regime) and does **not** reproduce the spatial
autocorrelation of the training patches — measured, and reported in the
vignette rather than hidden behind plausible-looking thumbnails. Use
`backend = "torch"`, which trains every layer by autograd and does
recover the structure.

📖 Vignette:
[`vignette("pilar9-diffusion-models")`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/articles/pilar9-diffusion-models.md).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Pillar 10 — Graph Neural Networks

### Motivation

Kriging assumes you know the covariance function; a random forest
assumes profiles are independent rows. Neither is right — profiles
inform each other through a relation that should be *learned*.

### Governing object

Graph attention \[[Veličković et
al. 2018](https://openreview.net/forum?id=rJXMpikCZ)\] over a k-NN
co-location graph of profiles:

``` math
e_{ij} = \mathrm{LeakyReLU}\!\big(\mathbf{a}^\top[W h_i \Vert W h_j]\big),
\qquad
\alpha_{ij} = \frac{\exp(e_{ij})}{\sum_{k \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \exp(e_{ik})}
```

The softmax is grouped per neighbourhood, and $`e_{ij}`$ depends on both
endpoints’ features — so two pairs at identical separation can receive
very different weights. That is what a fixed covariance function cannot
express.

``` r

g <- gnn_build_graph(profiles, k = 8L, feature_cols = feat,
                     edges = "spatial", self_loops = TRUE)

ens <- gnn_fit_ensemble(g, targets = profiles$soc,
                        train_mask = train_mask, n_ensemble = 5L)
```

Attention is trained by **analytic reverse-mode gradients** through the
grouped softmax — hand-derived, and checked against central finite
differences across several architectures in `test-pilar10-gat-grad.R`.
`train_mask` keeps every node in message passing while restricting the
loss to training nodes, so no test label reaches the optimiser.
[`gnn_fit_ensemble()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/gnn_fit_ensemble.md)
averages seeds so the published comparison against a 500-tree QRF is
ensemble-versus-ensemble rather than one model against a forest.

📖 Vignette:
[`vignette("pilar10-graph-attention")`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/articles/pilar10-graph-attention.md).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Unified uncertainty API (v1.6.0)

Through v1.5.0 each pillar quantified uncertainty in its own format.
v1.6.0 introduces **one class** — `edaphos_posterior` — and **one
calibration routine** —
[`uncertainty_calibrate()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/uncertainty_calibrate.md)
— that work identically for every pillar.

``` mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph NATIVE["Per-pillar native objects"]
        N1[P1 bootstrap<br/>effect vector]
        N2[P2 MCMC<br/>4 chains]
        N3[P3 ensemble +<br/>Kalman posterior]
        N4[P4 fine-tune<br/>ensemble]
        N5[P5 QRF<br/>quantile grid]
        N6[P6 Q-KRR<br/>GP variance]
    end
    subgraph UNI["edaphos_posterior"]
        ADAPT["samples / mean / sd<br/>+ method + query_type<br/>+ units + metadata"]
    end
    subgraph DIAG["uncertainty_calibrate()"]
        CRPS["CRPS"]
        PICP["PICP @ p"]
        MPIW["MPIW @ p"]
        REL["reliability curve"]
        RMSE["point RMSE"]
    end

    N1 -->|as_edaphos_posterior| ADAPT
    N2 -->|as_edaphos_posterior| ADAPT
    N3 -->|as_edaphos_posterior| ADAPT
    N4 -->|as_edaphos_posterior| ADAPT
    N5 -->|as_edaphos_posterior| ADAPT
    N6 -->|as_edaphos_posterior| ADAPT
    ADAPT --> CRPS
    ADAPT --> PICP
    ADAPT --> MPIW
    ADAPT --> REL
    ADAPT --> RMSE
```

Three lines of code are now enough to calibrate any pillar:

``` r

post <- causal_effect_posterior(data, dag, exposure, outcome, B = 500L)
cal  <- uncertainty_calibrate(post, truth = observed_effects)
autoplot(post)                       # ggplot2 figure by query type
```

### Native-query calibration (v1.7.1)

Evaluating each pillar **in its natural domain** — not forced into a
shared map query — gives the scientifically honest table:

| Pillar    | Native query           |   n |  CRPS | PICP (90%) | MPIW (90%) |  RMSE |
|:----------|:-----------------------|----:|------:|-----------:|-----------:|------:|
| P1 Causal | effect β (g/kg per mm) |  40 | 0.004 |  **0.775** |      0.020 | 0.007 |
| P2 PIML   | depth profile y(z)     |   9 | 1.971 |      0.778 |      6.608 | 4.096 |
| P3 4D     | future map NDVI(t★)    | 100 | 0.366 |  **0.700** |      1.268 | 0.637 |
| P4 Found. | 5-fold spatial CV      | 250 | 7.621 |      0.268 |      8.353 | 12.41 |
| **P5 AL** | held-out map           |  71 | 6.375 |  **0.930** |     37.816 | 12.86 |
| P6 Q-KRR  | held-out regression    |  75 | 8.203 |  **0.840** |     35.632 | 16.94 |

**How to read this table.** The 90% nominal PICP should be close to
0.90. **P5 AL (0.93) and P6 Q-KRR (0.84) are the best-calibrated**
spatial-query pillars; P1 (0.78) and P3 (0.70) are acceptable in their
own domains despite small n. Two rows flag real failure modes, both
reported rather than papered over. **P4’s 0.27** comes from naïve
ensembles of `ranger` heads underestimating epistemic SD, because
`ranger` already marginalises over trees. **P2’s 0.78** is the residue
of two corrections. The row used to read 0.71 with an RMSE of 0.83,
measured by leaving one horizon out of a seven-point profile that had
been typed in by hand; on a real nine-horizon WoSIS profile reaching 550
cm the same procedure gave 0.44. Two things were wrong with that number
and both are fixed. The interval being scored excluded observation
noise, so a mean-function interval was being asked to cover a measured
value it structurally cannot — restoring it takes the coverage to 0.67.
And the likelihood was Gaussian on g/kg, which puts predictive mass
below zero and weights every horizon by the same absolute error; a
lognormal takes it to 0.78 and removes the negative draws entirely. The
pedogenetic ODE is still overconfident at a nominal 0.90, and that is
now the honest residual rather than an artefact of how it was scored.
See
[`vignette("capstone-cerrado-campaign")`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/articles/capstone-cerrado-campaign.md)
§10 for the side-by-side comparison with the naïve unified-query table
and its caveats.

📖 Vignette:
[`vignette("uncertainty-unified")`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/articles/uncertainty-unified.md).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Capstone vignette (v1.7.0)

[`vignette("capstone-cerrado-campaign")`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/articles/capstone-cerrado-campaign.md)
is the flagship of v1.7.0 — a ~900-line narrative that puts the pillars
to work on a single decision: *where should we place 8 new field samples
in the Cerrado?*

### What it contains

- 📊 **12 figures** (ODE profile posteriors, EnKF gain maps,
  foundation-model SD maps, AL selection map, quantum-kernel
  decomposition, final decision map).
- 📋 **6 tables** (LLM-extracted claims, causal effects, ODE parameters,
  AL selection, calibration diagnostic, decision matrix).
- 🔁 **1 flowchart** of the six-pillar pipeline.
- 📐 **Full LaTeX derivations** of the pedogenetic ODE and the
  Gaspari-Cohn taper.
- 📚 **Citations tied back to [Zhang & Wadoux
  (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1111/ejss.70284)** at every pillar.

### The decision matrix

For each of the 8 sites, the vignette reports:

| column        | Pilar | Meaning                                          |
|:--------------|:-----:|:-------------------------------------------------|
| `score_p5`    |   5   | Hybrid AL score (uncertainty + diversity)        |
| `qkrr_ep`     |   6   | Q-KRR epistemic SD                               |
| `enkf_gain`   |   3   | Kalman gain magnitude at the site                |
| `found_sd`    |   4   | Foundation ensemble SD                           |
| `map_effect`  |   1   | Backdoor-adjusted MAP → COS direct effect        |
| `ode_pred`    |   2   | ODE-predicted topsoil SOC (sanity check)         |
| `final_score` |  1-6  | Weighted mean (weights declared in the vignette) |

The narrative then justifies each ranked site causally:

> **Site 1.** High EnKF gain (P3) indicates that SOC dynamics are
> changing fast here; high foundation-model SD (P4) confirms that the
> representation space is under-sampled. The ODE (P2) shows that $`k_1`$
> carries 2× above-average posterior variance in this cell — a new
> sample here directly reduces uncertainty about the decomposition
> process.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Benchmarks on real data

As of **v1.3.1** every performance claim against the classical
regression-tree state of the art is backed by a reproducible real-data
benchmark. The canonical case study runs on **1 095 real Cerrado topsoil
profiles** pulled live from [WoSIS
2019](https://essd.copernicus.org/articles/12/299/2020/) ([Batjes et
al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-12-299-2020), CC-BY-4.0),
evaluated by **5-fold spatial cross-validation** (k-means on
coordinates), with covariates from SoilGrids 250 m, WorldClim 2.1, SRTM
30-arcsec, and ESA WorldCover 2020.

| Method | n | RMSE (g/kg) | MAE (g/kg) | R² | PICP @ 95 | Interval score |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **B1** `ranger` QRF — 56 covariates | 1095 | **13.51** | 7.72 | **0.219** | 0.944 | **65.8** |
| **B2** `ranger` + `gstat` residual kriging | 893\* | 14.01 | 7.93 | 0.205 | **0.945** | 79.9 |
| **E** `ranger` + MoCo v1 embedding | 923\* | 14.07 | 7.95 | 0.157 | 0.940 | 71.7 |

\* Kriging drops test points whose variogram-range disk misses the
training cloud; the foundation stack drops points within 16 pixels of
the Cerrado raster edge.

**Honest reading.** R² ≈ 0.22 is in line with published regional
Brazilian / Cerrado SOC DSM. Residual kriging neither gains accuracy nor
costs calibration: it *loses* 0.014 R² against B1 (0.205 vs 0.219) and
its PICP is indistinguishable (0.945 vs 0.944). An earlier version of
this table reported the opposite on both counts — a +0.01 R² gain bought
with a PICP of 0.82 — and that was an artefact: B2’s training residuals
were formed from IN-SAMPLE forest predictions, which are too small by
about 4x, so the kriged correction and its variance were both
understated and B2’s intervals came out too narrow. With out-of-bag
predictions the intervals are right, the PICP recovers, and the apparent
accuracy gain disappears with it. The **plain QRF is still the
calibration champion**, now on a wider margin in interval score rather
than in PICP. The MoCo v1 embedding does not yet beat B1 on this dataset
— v1 was trained for only 20 k InfoNCE steps (10% of the canonical MoCo
v2 budget); v2 is in training, v1.3.2 will re-benchmark.

Reproduce with

``` bash
Rscript data-raw/case_cerrado_prepare.R   # ~60 min, downloads ~2 GB
Rscript data-raw/case_cerrado_run.R       # ~3 min
```

or read the pre-computed `.rds` shipped at
`inst/extdata/case_cerrado_results.rds` and rebuild every plot via
[`vignette("case-cerrado-end-to-end")`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/articles/case-cerrado-end-to-end.md).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Bundled datasets

### `br_cerrado` — 45 × 45 synthetic surrogate

A reproducible, offline, ~30 km × 30 km area near Brasília.

| Column   | Description                                    |
|----------|------------------------------------------------|
| `x, y`   | Longitude / latitude (WGS 84, decimal degrees) |
| `elev`   | Elevation (m a.s.l.)                           |
| `slope`  | Slope (degrees)                                |
| `twi`    | Topographic Wetness Index                      |
| `map_mm` | Mean annual precipitation (mm yr⁻¹)            |
| `ndvi`   | Dry-season NDVI (0–1)                          |
| `soc`    | **Target** — SOC, 0–5 cm (g kg⁻¹)              |

### `inst/extdata` real-data bundles (CC-BY-4.0)

| File | Size | What it holds | Used by |
|:---|---:|:---|:---|
| `case_cerrado_results.rds` | ~1 MB | QRF/kriging/MoCo benchmark (§Benchmarks) | `case-cerrado-end-to-end` |
| `causal_cerrado_real.rds` | ~2 MB | 1 095 WoSIS profiles + DAG + identified effects | `pilar1-causal-real` |
| `temporal_cerrado_results.rds` | ~195 KB | 2° MODIS × POWER 4D cube + ConvLSTM ensemble + EnKF analysis | `pilar3-4d-real` |
| `capstone_campaign_results.rds` | ~543 KB | 6-pillar integrated bundle for the v1.7.0 capstone | `capstone-cerrado-campaign` |
| `capstone_native_calibration.rds` | ~741 KB | Native-query calibration per pillar (v1.7.1 hotfix) | `capstone-cerrado-campaign` §10 |
| `causal_discovery_results.rds` | ~2 KB | Expert × LLM × data-driven DAG benchmark (v1.7.2) | `causal-discovery-trio` |
| `cerrado_gold_standard_v1.jsonl` | ~16 KB | 30 Cerrado abstracts × 72 annotated causal claims (v1.8.0 seed) | `llm-kg-benchmark` |
| `cerrado_gold_standard_v1_draft.jsonl` | ~20 KB | Gemma-4-style draft used by the annotation reviewer (v1.8.1 demo) | `llm-annotation-workflow` |
| `causal_iv_cerrado.rds` | ~12 KB | 2SLS instrumental-variable benchmark (v1.9.0): synthetic DGP + 1 095 Cerrado | `pilar1-pilar4-iv` |
| `causal_iv_cerrado_real.rds` | ~1 KB | Real-encoder IV benchmark: 1 081 embeddings; Sargan PARTIAL (see below) | `pilar1-pilar4-iv` §7 |
| `causal_sensitivity_cerrado.rds` | ~142 KB | Cinelli-Hazlett RV + bias-contour grid (v1.9.2) | `pilar1-pilar4-iv` §8 |
| `quantum_foundation_cerrado.rds` | ~1 KB | Pilar 4 x Pilar 6 benchmark: 5-fold spatial CV of 4 regressors (v2.0.0) | `pilar4-pilar6-quantum` |
| `llm_benchmark_results.rds` | ~10 KB | Gemma 4 × GPT × Claude benchmark bundle (P/R/F1, κ, cost, latency) | `llm-kg-benchmark` |
| `cerrado_abstracts.jsonl` | ~40 KB | 10 curated Cerrado-pedology abstracts | `pilar1-causal` |
| `cerrado_claims.jsonl` | ~25 KB | Gemma-4-extracted causal claims from the 10 abstracts | `pilar1-causal` |
| `cerrado_claims_real_corpus.jsonl` | ~400 KB | **100-abstract production corpus** (OpenAlex + SciELO) | `data-raw/run_large_corpus.R` |

The tagged release is archived on Zenodo with a DOI; the real-data
bundles ship inside it, in `inst/extdata/`, rather than carrying DOIs of
their own.

## Vignettes

``` r

browseVignettes("edaphos")
```

| Vignette | Scope |
|----|----|
| `pilar1-causal` | Backdoor adjustment in a pedogenetic DAG; naive vs. causal estimator on `br_cerrado`. |
| `pilar2-piml-profile` | Parametric ODE + Neural ODE of the depth profile on [`aqp::sp4`](https://ncss-tech.github.io/aqp/reference/sp4.html); Pillar 2 × 5 physics gate. |
| `pilar3-4d-soc` | Stacked ConvLSTM forecasting of the synthetic SOC cube; optional mass-balance physics loss. |
| `pilar4-simclr-embeddings` | Contrastive pre-training on raster patches; embeddings as auxiliary AL covariates. |
| `pilar5-active-learning` | Formal derivation of the hybrid query policy on the classic `meuse` dataset. |
| `pilar6-quantum` | Pure-R ZZFeatureMap simulator + quantum-kernel Gram matrix + Quantum KRR on binary SOC classification. |
| `uncertainty-unified` | Unified `edaphos_posterior` class + single calibration diagnostic, applied at v1.6.0 to the six pillars that existed then. |
| 🏆 `capstone-cerrado-campaign` | **v1.7.0 capstone**: the six pillars of that release, integrated in a Cerrado sampling-campaign decision. |
| `causal-discovery-trio` | **v1.7.2**: expert vs. LLM-augmented vs. data-driven (bnlearn hc / tabu / pc-stable) DAGs on 1 095 WoSIS Cerrado — SHD matrix + sensitivity of the adjustment set. |
| 🛠️ `llm-annotation-workflow` | **v1.8.1+**: pre-annotation + Shiny review workflow (with DAG preview, dark mode and Zenodo export from v1.8.2) to scale gold-standard from 72 to 300+ claims. |
| 🔗 `pilar1-pilar4-iv` | **v1.9.0+**: 2SLS instrumental variables using foundation-model embeddings; v1.9.1 adds real-encoder extraction (`foundation_embed_at_coords`); the Sargan test passes for one exposure of three and is reported as partial; v1.9.2 adds Cinelli-Hazlett sensitivity analysis. |
| 🌀 `pilar4-pilar6-quantum` | **v2.0.0**: quantum kernel over foundation-model embeddings — Pilar 4 × Pilar 6 fusion with 5-fold spatial-CV benchmark vs ranger / RBF / Q-KRR baselines. |
| `case-cerrado-end-to-end` | Real WoSIS benchmark: QRF vs. kriging vs. MoCo embedding (v1.3.1). |

Each vignette is written in the style of a short methods paper —
abstract, numbered sections with LaTeX derivations, shared BibTeX
bibliography (`vignettes/references.bib`).

## Testing and continuous integration

- **2 192 passing expectations** across 601 `test_that` blocks in 92
  test files (`testthat`), measured on aarch64-apple-darwin23, R 4.6.1.
  One expectation is skipped here, because its optional dependency is
  absent; every skip is an explicit `skip_if_not_installed()` gate.
- **Gated dependencies:** `torch`, `dagitty`, `bnlearn`, `dbarts`,
  `reticulate`, `terra`, `igraph`.
- **`R CMD check --as-cran`:** `2 NOTEs` at commit `8e725b9`. The
  per-item breakdown, including which items are package defects and
  which are artefacts of the checking machine, is in
  [`cran-comments.md`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/cran-comments.md);
  the log itself is committed at
  [`tools/status/check.log`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/tools/status/check.log).
- **CI:** GitHub Actions matrix on `macos-latest / R release`,
  `windows-latest / R release`, `ubuntu-latest / R devel`,
  `ubuntu-latest / R release`, `ubuntu-latest / R oldrel-1`,
  `ubuntu-latest / R release`. 1 of these 6 legs installs libtorch, so
  the torch-gated tests execute in CI rather than skipping.
- These figures are generated by `tools/status/patch-readme-metrics.R`
  from a real test run and a real check log. Do not edit them by hand.

> \[Software\]. <https://github.com/HugoMachadoRodrigues/edaphos>

# Package index

## Pilar 1 — Causal AI

Backdoor adjustment, LLM-driven Knowledge Graphs, causal discovery,
effect posteriors.

- [`causal_4d_plot()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/causal_4d_plot.md)
  : Plot a time-varying causal effect trajectory

- [`causal_adjustment_set()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/causal_adjustment_set.md)
  : Suggest a backdoor-adjustment set from a DAG

- [`causal_augment_dag()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/causal_augment_dag.md)
  : Augment a base DAG with edges from a Knowledge Graph

- [`causal_augment_diff()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/causal_augment_diff.md)
  : Diff between a base DAG and an augmented DAG

- [`causal_cerrado_dag()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/causal_cerrado_dag.md)
  :

  DAG tailored to the bundled Cerrado dataset (`br_cerrado`)

- [`causal_cerrado_real_dag()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/causal_cerrado_real_dag.md)
  : Real-data Cerrado pedogenetic DAG

- [`causal_clorpt_dag()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/causal_clorpt_dag.md)
  : Canonical CLORPT pedogenetic DAG

- [`causal_corpus_deduplicate()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/causal_corpus_deduplicate.md)
  : Deduplicate a corpus by DOI or title

- [`causal_corpus_openalex()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/causal_corpus_openalex.md)
  : Query the OpenAlex corpus

- [`causal_corpus_scielo()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/causal_corpus_scielo.md)
  : Query the SciELO literature corpus

- [`causal_dag_test()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/causal_dag_test.md)
  : Test a DAG against the conditional independencies it implies

- [`causal_effect_bootstrap()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/causal_effect_bootstrap.md)
  : Block-bootstrap the backdoor-adjusted direct effect

- [`causal_effect_posterior()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/causal_effect_posterior.md)
  : Posterior distribution of a backdoor-adjusted direct effect

- [`causal_effect_time_varying()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/causal_effect_time_varying.md)
  : Time-varying causal effect beta(t) over a sliding window

- [`causal_effect_trend_test()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/causal_effect_trend_test.md)
  : Mann-Kendall trend test on a beta(t) trajectory

- [`causal_estimate_effect()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/causal_estimate_effect.md)
  : Estimate a causal effect using DAG-guided backdoor adjustment

- [`causal_iv_first_stage()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/causal_iv_first_stage.md)
  : First-stage regression diagnostics for an IV design

- [`causal_iv_fit_2sls()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/causal_iv_fit_2sls.md)
  : Two-stage least squares (2SLS) instrumental variable estimator

## Pilar 6 — Quantum ML

ZZFeatureMap, Quantum KRR, Qiskit VQE, organo-mineral Hamiltonians.

- [`quantum_hamiltonian_ising_1d()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/quantum_hamiltonian_ising_1d.md)

- [`quantum_hamiltonian_organo_mineral()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/quantum_hamiltonian_organo_mineral.md)

- [`quantum_ibmq_available()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/quantum_ibmq_available.md)
  : Check whether an IBM Quantum backend is reachable

- [`quantum_ibmq_backends()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/quantum_ibmq_backends.md)
  : List IBM Quantum backends available to the current account

- [`quantum_ibmq_least_busy()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/quantum_ibmq_least_busy.md)
  : Pick the least-busy operational IBM Quantum backend

- [`quantum_ibmq_submit()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/quantum_ibmq_submit.md)
  : Submit a single expectation-value PUB to IBM Quantum hardware

- [`quantum_kernel()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/quantum_kernel.md)
  : Quantum kernel Gram matrix via ZZFeatureMap overlap

- [`quantum_krr_fit()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/quantum_krr_fit.md)
  : Fit a Quantum Kernel Ridge Regression (Pillar 6)

- [`quantum_krr_posterior()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/quantum_krr_posterior.md)
  : GP-equivalent posterior for a Quantum Kernel Ridge Regression fit

- [`quantum_nature_available()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/quantum_nature_available.md)
  : Check whether the qiskit-nature + PySCF stack is available

- [`quantum_nature_total_energy()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/quantum_nature_total_energy.md)
  : Total molecular energy from an active-space VQE result

- [`quantum_scale()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/quantum_scale.md)
  :

  Rescale a covariate matrix into `[lower, upper]` column-wise

- [`quantum_vqe_exact()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/quantum_vqe_exact.md)
  : Exact ground-state energy via classical diagonalisation

- [`quantum_vqe_fit()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/quantum_vqe_fit.md)
  : Variational Quantum Eigensolver (Pillar 6 main entry point)

## Pilar 7 — Bayesian Hierarchical Spatial (v2.3.0+)

Gaussian process + Gibbs sampler (R fast-path / RcppArmadillo /
spBayes).

- [`bhs_fit()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/bhs_fit.md)
  : Fit a Bayesian hierarchical spatial linear model (Pilar 7)
- [`predict(`*`<edaphos_bhs>`*`)`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/predict.edaphos_bhs.md)
  : Predict at new sites from a fitted Bayesian hierarchical spatial
  model

## Pilar 8 — Neural Operators (v2.4.0+)

DeepONet + FNO over depth function space.

- [`no_deeponet_fit()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/no_deeponet_fit.md)
  : Fit a DeepONet for depth-profile operators
- [`no_fno_fit()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/no_fno_fit.md)
  : Fit a 1-D Fourier Neural Operator for depth-profile operators

## Pilar 9 — Diffusion Models (v2.5.0+)

DDPM with cosine schedule + ancestral sampling.

- [`dm_cosine_schedule()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/dm_cosine_schedule.md)
  : Build a DDPM noise schedule
- [`dm_fit()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/dm_fit.md)
  : Train a tiny DDPM on a collection of soil-map patches
- [`dm_sample()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/dm_sample.md)
  : Sample new soil-map patches from a trained DDPM

## Pilar 10 — Graph Attention Networks (v2.6.0+)

k-NN co-location graphs + multi-head attention; v3.6.0 sparse.

- [`gnn_build_graph()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/gnn_build_graph.md)
  : Build a k-NN co-location graph from a profile frame
- [`gnn_causal_discovery()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/gnn_causal_discovery.md)
  : Graph-based causal discovery (Pilar 10 x Pilar 1)
- [`gnn_embed()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/gnn_embed.md)
  : Node-level embeddings from a fitted GAT
- [`gnn_fit()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/gnn_fit.md)
  : Fit a Graph Attention Network on a WoSIS-style co-location graph
- [`gnn_fit_ensemble()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/gnn_fit_ensemble.md)
  : Seed ensemble of GAT fits

## Cross-pillar bridges (v1.9.x + v2.0.0 + v3.0.0)

Foundation embeddings as causal instruments; quantum kernels over
foundation embeddings; six v3.0.0 bridges (P7/8/9 x P5 + P10 x P1 + P2 x
P3 + P6 x P10).

- [`qf_embed_reduce()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/qf_embed_reduce.md)
  : Reduce foundation-model embeddings to PCs and scale to quantum range
- [`qf_kernel_compare()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/qf_kernel_compare.md)
  : Compare quantum, RBF, and linear kernels on the same feature set
- [`qf_krr_benchmark()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/qf_krr_benchmark.md)
  : Benchmark quantum-foundation KRR against classical baselines
- [`qf_krr_fit()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/qf_krr_fit.md)
  : Quantum Kernel Ridge Regression on foundation embeddings
- [`qf_krr_on_gat_embeddings()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/qf_krr_on_gat_embeddings.md)
  : Quantum KRR over GAT node embeddings (Pilar 6 x Pilar 10)
- [`al_query_batchbald()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/al_query_batchbald.md)
  : BatchBALD information-theoretic batch acquisition
- [`al_query_bhs()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/al_query_bhs.md)
  : Bayesian Hierarchical Active Learning (Pilar 7 x Pilar 5)
- [`al_query_causal()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/al_query_causal.md)
  : Causal Active Learning: query the next sample(s) that most reduce
  the uncertainty of a targeted causal effect
- [`al_query_diffusion()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/al_query_diffusion.md)
  : Diffusion-posterior-driven AL (Pilar 9 x Pilar 5)
- [`al_query_neural_operator()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/al_query_neural_operator.md)
  : Causal-driven AL via Neural Operator disagreement (Pilar 8 x Pilar
  5)
- [`al_query_temporal()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/al_query_temporal.md)
  : Temporal Active Learning: rank candidate cells by their Kalman gain
  norm after the latest EnKF assimilation
- [`gnn_causal_discovery()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/gnn_causal_discovery.md)
  : Graph-based causal discovery (Pilar 10 x Pilar 1)
- [`temporal_piml_loss()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/temporal_piml_loss.md)
  : Physics-informed ConvLSTM mass-balance loss (Pilar 2 x Pilar 3)

## Unified uncertainty API (v1.6.0)

Common edaphos_posterior class + single calibration diagnostic.

- [`uncertainty_calibrate()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/uncertainty_calibrate.md)
  :

  Calibration diagnostics for an `edaphos_posterior`

- [`uncertainty_plot_reliability()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/uncertainty_plot_reliability.md)
  : Reliability diagram from a calibration result

- [`edaphos_posterior()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/edaphos_posterior.md)
  : Unified posterior object for the edaphos pillars

- [`as_edaphos_posterior()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/as_edaphos_posterior.md)
  :

  Coerce a native pillar object to `edaphos_posterior`

- [`autoplot.edaphos_posterior()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/autoplot.edaphos_posterior.md)
  :

  Default ggplot for an `edaphos_posterior`

- [`edaphos_bias()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/edaphos_bias.md)
  : Mean bias (observed minus predicted)

- [`edaphos_ece()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/edaphos_ece.md)
  : Expected calibration error (ECE) for a regression reliability
  diagram

- [`edaphos_interval_score()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/edaphos_interval_score.md)
  : Interval score (Gneiting and Raftery 2007)

- [`edaphos_mae()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/edaphos_mae.md)
  : Mean absolute error

- [`edaphos_metrics_summary()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/edaphos_metrics_summary.md)
  : Summarise a pointwise + interval prediction against observations

- [`edaphos_nse()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/edaphos_nse.md)
  : Skill against an explicit null predictor

- [`edaphos_picp()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/edaphos_picp.md)
  : Prediction-interval coverage probability (PICP)

- [`edaphos_provenance()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/edaphos_provenance.md)
  : Provenance for a generated data bundle

- [`edaphos_provenance_check()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/edaphos_provenance_check.md)
  : Check a bundle against the script that produced it

- [`edaphos_r2()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/edaphos_r2.md)
  : Coefficient of determination (Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency)

- [`edaphos_rmse()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/edaphos_rmse.md)
  : Root-mean-square error

- [`edaphos_zenodo_release()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/edaphos_zenodo_release.md)
  : Build a Zenodo-ready release bundle for the edaphos package

## Benchmark wrappers (v3.1.0)

Plug-and-play wrappers for the 6-pilar WoSIS Cerrado benchmark.

- [`benchmark_fit_p10_gat()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/benchmark_fit_p10_gat.md)
  : Benchmark wrapper: Pilar 10 – GAT seed-ensemble on k-NN graph
- [`benchmark_fit_p1_causal()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/benchmark_fit_p1_causal.md)
  : Benchmark wrapper: Pilar 1 – DAG-adjusted OLS + parametric bootstrap
- [`benchmark_fit_p6_quantum()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/benchmark_fit_p6_quantum.md)
  : Benchmark wrapper: Pilar 6 – bootstrap-ensembled quantum KRR
- [`spatial_block_folds()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/spatial_block_folds.md)
  : Spatially blocked cross-validation folds with a buffer

## LLM-KG production pipeline (v3.10.0)

Resumable 10k+ abstract orchestrator + Ollama pre-flight.

- [`llm_kg_ollama_check()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/llm_kg_ollama_check.md)
  : Check whether a local Ollama server is reachable
- [`llm_kg_pipeline_run()`](https://hugomachadorodrigues.github.io/edaphos/reference/llm_kg_pipeline_run.md)
  : Run the Pilar 1 LLM-KG pipeline on a (potentially large) corpus
